source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 11 (PDF 251-260, printed 248-257); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 11 (Special Theory of Relativity), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Classical physics based on Newton's laws failed to explain phenomena involving:

options.text: extremely small particles or very high velocities
bodies at rest on the Earth

blocks.explanation: New experiments showed that classical physics could not explain extremely small particles or very high velocities (11.1).

book_ref.quote: could not explain phenomena involving extremely small particles or very high velocities

blocks.prompt: 2 Einstein introduced the special theory of relativity in the year:
blocks.explanation: The Special Theory of Relativity was introduced by Albert Einstein in 1905 (11.1).

book_ref.quote: Albert Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity, introduced in 1905

blocks.prompt: 3 The special theory of relativity resolved the conflicts between classical mechanics and:
blocks.explanation: The theory resolved the conflicts between classical mechanics and electromagnetic theory (11.1).

book_ref.quote: resolved the conflicts between classical mechanics and electromagnetic theory

blocks.prompt: 4 A ball thrown to your right appears to move to the left of a person facing you. This shows that direction is:
blocks.explanation: Right for one observer is left for the observer facing him, so direction is a relative concept (11.1).

book_ref.quote: This illustrates that direction is a relative concept.

blocks.prompt: 5 The walls of a moving train seem stationary to its passengers but moving to a person on the ground. This shows that:

options.text: all motions are relative to the observer
the train is absolutely at rest
the train is absolutely in motion

blocks.explanation: We cannot say whether an object is absolutely at rest or in motion; all motions are relative to the observer or frame (11.1).

book_ref.quote: all motions are relative to the observer or to the reference frame being used

blocks.prompt: 6 A ball is dropped inside a train that is at rest. Its horizontal distance travelled is:

options.text: equal to the height of fall
half the length of the compartment

blocks.explanation: With the train stationary, the ball's horizontal velocity is zero, so its horizontal distance is also zero (11.1, case a).

book_ref.quote: the horizontal velocity of the ball will be zero

blocks.prompt: 7 A ball is dropped in a train moving with uniform velocity. An observer standing outside sees the ball follow a:
blocks.explanation: The ball keeps the train's horizontal velocity vₒ and behaves like a projectile for the outside observer (11.1, case b).

book_ref.quote: an observer outside the train will see the ball following a projectile path

blocks.prompt: 8 For an observer inside a train moving with uniform velocity, a dropped ball lands:

options.text: directly below the point of release
ahead of the point of release
on the side wall of the compartment

blocks.explanation: The train, the observer and the ball all move the same horizontal distance vₒt, so the ball lands directly below (11.1).

book_ref.quote: Therefore, the observer inside the train sees that the ball falls to a point on the floor directly below

blocks.prompt: 9 A train moves with a uniform velocity of 15 m s⁻¹. A ball dropped in it takes 0.4 s to reach the floor. For an observer on the ground, the horizontal distance travelled by the ball is:
blocks.explanation: Horizontal distance = vₒt = 15 × 0.4 = 6.0 m (11.1, case b).

book_ref.quote: It travels a horizontal distance vₒt in time t it takes for the ball to reach the floor.

blocks.prompt: 10 A frame of reference is:

options.text: any coordinate system relative to which measurements are taken
a frame that is always at rest
a frame that is always accelerating
the walls of a laboratory only

blocks.explanation: A frame of reference is any coordinate system relative to which measurements are taken (11.2).

book_ref.quote: a frame of reference is any coordinate system relative to which measurements are taken

blocks.prompt: 11 The position of a spaceship is described relative to:
blocks.explanation: A coordinate system based on distant stars is the frame of reference for a spaceship (11.2).

book_ref.quote: The position of a spaceship can be described relative to the positions of distant stars

blocks.prompt: 12 An experiment is performed inside a moving train. The frame of reference for the measurements is:
blocks.explanation: When the experiment is performed in a moving train, the train becomes the frame of reference (11.2).

book_ref.quote: If the same experiment is performed in a moving train, the train becomes the frame of reference

blocks.prompt: 13 A frame of reference in which the law of inertia is valid is called:
blocks.explanation: An inertial frame is a coordinate system in which the law of inertia is valid (11.2).

book_ref.quote: An inertial frame of reference is defined as a coordinate system in which the law of inertia is valid

blocks.prompt: 14 A frame of reference moving with uniform velocity relative to an inertial frame is:
blocks.explanation: Any frame moving with uniform velocity relative to an inertial frame is also an inertial frame, like a uniformly moving car (11.2).

book_ref.quote: any frame of reference moving with uniform velocity relative to an inertial frame is also an inertial frame

blocks.prompt: 15 Which of the following is a non-inertial frame of reference?

options.text: A car moving with uniform velocity
A train at rest on its track
A car that is suddenly stopped
A frame moving uniformly relative to an inertial frame

blocks.explanation: When a car is suddenly stopped or accelerated, a body inside no longer stays at rest; an accelerated frame is non-inertial (11.2).

book_ref.quote: if the moving car is suddenly stopped or accelerated, the body inside no longer remains at rest

blocks.prompt: 16 Strictly, the Earth is a non-inertial frame because it rotates and revolves. It is still treated as an inertial frame because:

options.text: it does not move at all
the law of inertia does not apply on it

blocks.explanation: The Earth is often treated as an inertial frame due to its relatively small acceleration (11.2).

book_ref.quote: it is often treated as an inertial frame due to its relatively small acceleration

blocks.prompt: 17 Relativity is the study of how:

options.text: observers in moving frames of reference perceive the world
light is produced by hot bodies
heat flows from hot to cold bodies

blocks.explanation: The box defines relativity as the study of the way observers from moving frames of reference perceive the world (11.2).

book_ref.quote: Relativity is the study of the way in which observers from moving frame of reference affect your perception of the world.

blocks.prompt: 18 The special theory of relativity deals with:
blocks.explanation: The special theory addresses inertial (non-accelerating) frames; the general theory deals with accelerating frames (11.3).

book_ref.quote: The special theory of relativity addresses problems involving inertial (non-accelerating) frames of reference.

blocks.prompt: 19 Frames of reference that are accelerating relative to one another are dealt with by:
blocks.explanation: The general theory of relativity deals with frames accelerating relative to one another (11.3).

book_ref.quote: that deals with problems involving frames of reference that are accelerating relative to one another

blocks.prompt: 20 The statement "the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames" is called the:
blocks.explanation: The first postulate is the Principle of Relativity: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames (11.3).

book_ref.quote: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames (Principle of Relativity).

blocks.prompt: 21 According to the second postulate, the speed of light in free space:

options.text: has the same value for all observers
depends on the motion of the source
depends on the motion of the observer
is greater for an observer moving towards the source

blocks.explanation: The speed of light in free space has the same value for all observers, regardless of the motion of source or observer (11.3).

book_ref.quote: regardless of the state of motion of the source or the observer (Principle of Constancy of Light)

blocks.prompt: 22 Light from the flashlight of a car moving with speed v is measured by the driver and by a man on the road. Compared with the driver, the man on the road measures its speed as:
blocks.explanation: Both observers measure the same speed c for the light from the car (11.3, Do You Know?).

book_ref.quote: is measured same by two observers, one moving in the car with speed v and other standing on the road

blocks.prompt: 23 The first postulate of special relativity implies that:

options.text: absolute uniform motion can always be detected
absolute uniform motion cannot be detected
the speed of light depends on the source
only the Earth is an inertial frame

blocks.explanation: If laws differed between frames, one could tell which is moving; since they do not, absolute uniform motion cannot be detected (11.3).

book_ref.quote: implying that there is no way to detect absolute uniform motion

blocks.prompt: 24 The value of the universal constant c used in this chapter is:
blocks.explanation: The speed of light in free space is a universal constant, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ (11.3).

book_ref.quote: the speed of light in free space is a universal constant, denoted as c

blocks.prompt: 25 Because the speed of light c is constant for all observers:
blocks.explanation: Since c is constant, space and time become relative (11.3).

book_ref.quote: Since c is constant, space and time become relative.

blocks.prompt: 26 A person in a train moving at constant velocity close to the speed of light holds a mirror at arm's length. The person:

options.text: sees his reflection late by a few seconds

blocks.explanation: No experiment can detect constant motion of the train relative to the person, so he sees his reflection as usual (11.3; book correction: the train moves at constant velocity, not at c).

book_ref.quote: no experiment can detect the constant motion of the train relative to the person inside it

blocks.prompt: 27 Two consequences of the postulates of special relativity, as seen by a stationary observer, are:

options.text: slowing down of moving clocks and contraction of moving lengths
speeding up of moving clocks and stretching of lengths
constant time and constant length in all frames
decrease of mass and increase of length

blocks.explanation: The postulates lead to the slowing down of clocks and contraction of lengths in moving frames as observed by a stationary observer (11.3).

book_ref.quote: the slowing down of clocks and the contraction of lengths in moving reference frames

blocks.prompt: 28 According to the special theory of relativity, time:

options.text: is the same for all observers
depends only on the mass of the clock
depends on the motion of the frame of reference

blocks.explanation: Time is not an absolute quantity; it depends on the motion of the frame of reference (11.3).

book_ref.quote: time is not an absolute quantity; it depends on the motion of the frame of reference

blocks.prompt: 29 The time interval between two events measured by an observer at rest in the frame of the events is called:
blocks.explanation: The interval tₒ measured by an observer stationary in the frame of the events is known as proper time (11.3).

book_ref.quote: This is known as proper time.

blocks.prompt: 30 In the relation t = tₒ/√(1 − v²/c²), the time t measured by a moving observer is:
blocks.explanation: √(1 − v²/c²) is always less than one, so t is greater than tₒ: time has dilated (11.3).

book_ref.quote: is always less than one, so t is greater than

blocks.prompt: 31 Time dilation applies to:

options.text: all timing processes: physical, chemical and biological

blocks.explanation: Time dilation applies to all timing processes, physical, chemical and biological; even aging slows at relativistic speeds (11.3).

book_ref.quote: This astonishing result applies to all timing processes

blocks.prompt: 32 A clock ticks once every 2.0 s in its own frame. What interval between ticks is measured by an observer moving at 0.6 c relative to the clock?

book_ref.quote: the time measured by the observer will not be

blocks.prompt: 33 An event takes 10 s as measured by a traveler in a spaceship moving at 0.8 c. For an observer outside, the same event takes:

book_ref.quote: the event takes one second as measured by the traveler

blocks.prompt: 34 An observer finds that a process in a frame moving past him at 0.6 c lasts 5.0 s. The proper time of the process is:

book_ref.quote: if the frame of events is moving with respect to the observer with a uniform relativistic velocity v

blocks.prompt: 35 At relativistic speeds, the aging process of the human body, as seen by a stationary observer:
blocks.explanation: Time dilation applies to biological processes too, so aging is slowed by motion at very high speeds (11.3).

book_ref.quote: Even the aging process of the human body is slowed by motion at very high speeds

blocks.prompt: 36 Compared with an observer on the Earth, an observer in a fast moving spaceship measures the distance from Earth to a star:
blocks.explanation: The distance appears smaller to the observer in the moving spaceship; this is length contraction (11.3).

book_ref.quote: would appear smaller than the distance measured by an observer on the Earth

blocks.prompt: 37 Length contraction occurs:

options.text: only perpendicular to the direction of motion
only along the direction of motion

blocks.explanation: Length contraction occurs only along the direction of motion; none is observed perpendicular to it (11.3).

book_ref.quote: Length contraction occurs only along the direction of motion

blocks.prompt: 38 A rod of length 1.0 m is held perpendicular to the direction of motion of a spaceship moving at 0.8 c. Its length measured by an observer at rest outside is:
blocks.explanation: No contraction is observed perpendicular to the direction of motion, so the length stays 1.0 m (11.3).

book_ref.quote: no such contraction is observed perpendicular to the direction of motion

blocks.prompt: 39 The length of an object measured by an observer at rest relative to it is called:
blocks.explanation: The length measured by an observer at rest relative to the object is called the proper length ℓₒ (11.3).

book_ref.quote: is called the proper length

blocks.prompt: 40 A rod 2.0 m long at rest moves along its length at 0.6 c relative to an observer. The observer measures its length as:

book_ref.quote: If an object and an observer are in relative motion with speed v

blocks.prompt: 41 A spaceship is 50 m long at rest. It moves at 0.8 c. A person inside the spaceship measures its length as:
blocks.explanation: The person inside is at rest relative to the spaceship, so he measures the proper length, 50 m (11.3). An outside observer would measure 50 × 0.6 = 30 m.

book_ref.quote: A person inside the train will measure its length as 100 metres.

blocks.prompt: 42 A spaceship is 50 m long at rest. It flies past an observer at 0.8 c. The observer measures its length as:

book_ref.quote: a person standing by the side of the track will observe the train to be only 60 metres long

blocks.prompt: 43 At what speed will a rod moving along its length appear to an observer at rest to be half of its proper length?

book_ref.quote: This effect is known as length contraction.

blocks.prompt: 44 According to the special theory of relativity, the mass of an object:
blocks.explanation: Mass is a variable quantity that depends on the object's speed (11.3).

book_ref.quote: the mass of an object is a variable quantity that depends on the object's speed

blocks.prompt: 45 The increase in the mass of an object at high speed indicates an increase in its:
blocks.explanation: The increase in mass indicates the increase in inertia; a greater force is needed to change its speed (11.3).

book_ref.quote: The increase in mass indicates the increase in inertia that an object has at high speeds.

blocks.prompt: 46 A material object cannot be accelerated to the speed of light because, as v approaches c, its mass:

options.text: stays equal to its rest mass
becomes half of its rest mass

blocks.explanation: As v → c, √(1 − v²/c²) → 0 so m → ∞; an infinite mass would need an infinite force, which is not available (11.3).

book_ref.quote: An infinite mass would require an infinite force to accelerate it.

blocks.prompt: 47 A body has a rest mass of 2.0 kg. Its mass when moving at 0.6 c is:

book_ref.quote: An object whose mass is measured at rest is called its rest mass

blocks.prompt: 48 At what speed does the mass of a particle become twice its rest mass?
blocks.explanation: m/mₒ = 2 means √(1 − v²/c²) = 0.5, so v²/c² = 0.75 and v = 0.866 c (11.3).

book_ref.quote: will have an increased mass m when observed to be moving at speed v

blocks.prompt: 49 The ratio m/mₒ for a body moving at 0.28 c is about:

book_ref.quote: As v approaches c, it requires a greater force to change the object's speed.

blocks.prompt: 50 Newton's laws are valid in everyday situations because everyday speeds are:

options.text: close to the speed of light
greater than the speed of light
extremely small compared to the speed of light

blocks.explanation: Even Earth's orbital speed (30 km s⁻¹) is tiny compared with 300,000 km s⁻¹, so Newton's laws hold (11.3).

book_ref.quote: This is why Newton's laws are valid in everyday situations.

blocks.prompt: 51 Using the chapter's values, Earth's orbital speed (30 km s⁻¹) is what fraction of the speed of light in free space (300,000 km s⁻¹)?
blocks.explanation: 30/300,000 = 1 × 10⁻⁴, so relativistic effects are negligible; they become prominent only near the speed of light (11.3).

book_ref.quote: relativistic effects become very prominent

blocks.prompt: 52 Whether two events at different places are simultaneous:

options.text: is the same for all observers
depends only on the distance between them
depends on the observer's frame of reference
depends on the mass of the observer

blocks.explanation: Events simultaneous for one observer are generally not simultaneous for an observer in another moving frame (11.3).

book_ref.quote: whether two events are seen as simultaneous depends on the observer's frame of reference

blocks.prompt: 53 In a train with light-operated doors, a traveler in the middle switches on the light. The traveler sees the two doors open:
blocks.explanation: Light travels forward and backward at equal speed and reaches both doors together, so the traveler sees them open simultaneously (11.3).

book_ref.quote: the traveler sees both doors opening simultaneously

blocks.prompt: 54 In the same light-operated door experiment, an observer outside the moving train sees:

options.text: the front door open before the back door
the back door open before the front door

blocks.explanation: The back door moves towards the light waves and the front door moves away, so the outside observer sees the back door open first (11.3).

book_ref.quote: an observer outside the train will see the back door open before the front door

blocks.prompt: 55 In a frame moving at constant velocity from which no other frame can be seen, you:

options.text: can always tell that you are moving
cannot know whether you are moving or at rest
can tell your speed by a pendulum
can tell you are at rest by dropping a ball

blocks.explanation: In such a frame there is no way to know whether you are moving or at rest (11.3, Interesting Information).

book_ref.quote: there is no way to know if you are moving or at rest

blocks.text: 11.4 The equivalence between mass and energy

blocks.prompt: 56 According to the special theory of relativity, mass and energy are:
blocks.explanation: Mass and energy are distinct entities but are interconvertible, related by E = mc² (11.4).

book_ref.quote: mass and energy are distinct entities but are interconvertible

blocks.prompt: 57 The energy equivalent of the mass of an object at rest is called its:
blocks.explanation: At rest, the energy equivalent of mₒ is the rest mass energy, Eₒ = mₒc² (11.4).

book_ref.quote: is called its rest mass energy

blocks.prompt: 58 The rest mass energy of 1.0 g of matter is (take c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹):

book_ref.quote: The total energy E and mass m of an object are related by the expression:

blocks.prompt: 59 In relativity, the kinetic energy of a moving object equals:

options.text: its total energy minus its rest mass energy
its total energy plus its rest mass energy

blocks.explanation: mc² − mₒc² is due to motion and is the kinetic energy (11.4).

book_ref.quote: is due to the motion, and it represents the kinetic energy of the mass

blocks.prompt: 60 A 1.0 kg body moves at 0.6 c. Its kinetic energy is (take c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹):

book_ref.quote: As mc² is greater than mₒc²

blocks.prompt: 61 Because c² is very large:

options.text: large changes in mass need small changes in energy
small changes in mass require very large changes in energy

blocks.explanation: From Δm = ΔE/c², a small change in mass corresponds to a very large change in energy (11.4).

book_ref.quote: small changes in mass require very large changes in energy

blocks.prompt: 62 In a reaction 4.5 × 10¹³ J of energy is released. The corresponding decrease in mass is (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹):

book_ref.quote: the change in mass m due to change in energy

blocks.prompt: 63 Mass changes are not noticed in everyday energy changes because:

options.text: the energy changes are too small to give measurable mass changes

blocks.explanation: In our everyday world energy changes are too small to provide measurable mass changes (11.4).

book_ref.quote: energy changes are too small to provide measurable mass changes

blocks.prompt: 64 The mass-energy relations of the chapter are found to agree exactly with energy and mass changes in:
blocks.explanation: Energy and mass changes in nuclear reactions are exactly in accordance with these equations (11.4).

book_ref.quote: energy and mass changes in nuclear reactions are found to be exactly in accordance

blocks.prompt: 65 A spaceship travels to a star at a high speed. From the Earth's point of view, the clocks on the spaceship:

options.text: run at the same rate as Earth clocks

blocks.explanation: From the Earth's point of view the spaceship clocks move slowly, so less time passes on the spaceship (11.5).

book_ref.quote: From the Earth's point of view, the clocks on the spaceship are moving slowly

blocks.prompt: 66 The occupants of a fast spaceship take less time to reach a star because, for them:

options.text: the speed of light has increased
the length of the journey has contracted
the star moves towards the Earth

blocks.explanation: For the occupants, the length of the journey has contracted, which they cover in less time (11.5).

book_ref.quote: For the spaceship occupants, the length of the journey has contracted

blocks.prompt: 67 A spaceship travels to a star at 0.6 c. Observers on the Earth find the journey takes 10 years. The occupants of the spaceship record:
blocks.explanation: Ship time = 10 × √(1 − 0.36) = 10 × 0.8 = 8 years, the same reasoning as the chapter's 8-year journey (11.5).

book_ref.quote: Let a spaceship be travelling to a star with half of the speed of light.

blocks.prompt: 68 Space is described in the chapter as:

options.text: a three-dimensional extent in which all objects and events occur
a measure of the sequence of events

blocks.explanation: Space is a three-dimensional extent in which all objects and events occur (11.5).

book_ref.quote: Space is said to be a three-dimensional extent in which all objects and events occur.

blocks.prompt: 69 In the theory of relativity, time is considered:
blocks.explanation: Time is not absolute; it is considered the fourth dimension (11.5).

book_ref.quote: In the theory of relativity, time is not absolute; it is considered the fourth dimension.

blocks.prompt: 70 Space-time is:

options.text: a mathematical model that unifies space and time into a single continuum
the distance travelled by light in one year
a region of space without time

blocks.explanation: Space-time is a mathematical model that unifies space and time into a single continuum (11.5).

book_ref.quote: a mathematical model that unifies space-time into a single continuum

blocks.prompt: 71 According to Einstein's view, the curvature of space-time around a body is deeper when the body:
blocks.explanation: Stars and planets curve space-time around themselves; the more massive the object, the deeper the curve (11.5).

book_ref.quote: The more massive the object, the deeper the curve.

blocks.prompt: 72 In curved space-time, bodies and light rays move along:
blocks.explanation: We do not speak of a force of gravity; bodies and light rays move along geodesics in curved space-time (11.5).

book_ref.quote: bodies and light rays move along geodesics

blocks.prompt: 73 Einstein's theory is considered an advancement over Newton's theory of gravity because it:

options.text: rejects the inverse square law completely
explains why gravity follows an inverse square law
gives different results for weak gravitational fields
applies only to light and not to bodies

blocks.explanation: Newton gave no explanation for the inverse square law; Einstein's theory also gives it (except in strong fields) and explains why (11.5).

book_ref.quote: but it explains why this is so

blocks.prompt: 74 Einstein's theory of gravity gives results different from Newton's theory only in:
blocks.explanation: It encompasses Newton's theory and gives the same results in all but very strong gravitational fields (11.5).

book_ref.quote: yields the same results as Newton's theory in all but very strong gravitational fields

blocks.prompt: 75 The bending of starlight by the Sun's gravity was measured during a solar eclipse in:
blocks.explanation: It was measured during the solar eclipse of 1919 and matched Einstein's theory rather than Newton's (11.5).

book_ref.quote: The bending of starlight caused by the Sun's gravity was measured during a solar eclipse in 1919.

blocks.prompt: 76 The bending of light around massive objects such as stars is described by:
blocks.explanation: Book correction: the effect of gravity on space and time and the bending of light are described by the general theory of relativity (11.5).

book_ref.quote: are described by Einstein's general theory of relativity

blocks.prompt: 77 Gravitational waves, disturbances in the curvature of space-time, were first detected in:
blocks.explanation: Gravitational waves were detected in 2015 and announced in 2016 (11.5).

book_ref.quote: These waves were detected in 2015 and announced in 2016.

blocks.prompt: 78 According to the chapter, time goes slower for you when you:

options.text: move faster or are close to a strong source of gravity
move slower or are far from gravity
stand still far from all masses
move in a circle at low speed

blocks.explanation: The faster you move or the closer you are to a strong source of gravity, the slower time goes for you (11.5).

book_ref.quote: The faster you are moving or close to a strong source of gravity, the slower the time goes for you.

blocks.prompt: 79 A pendulum has a period of 1.5 s in its own frame. What period is measured by an observer moving at 0.6 c relative to it?

book_ref.quote: The period of a pendulum is measured to be 3.0 s in the inertial reference frame of the pendulum.

blocks.prompt: 80 A bar of proper length 4.0 m lies along the x-axis and moves along it at 0.6 c. A stationary observer measures its length as:
blocks.explanation: ℓ = ℓₒ√(1 − v²/c²) = 4.0 × 0.8 = 3.2 m (Example 11.2 method, 11.5).

book_ref.quote: A bar 1.0 m in length and located along x-axis moves with a speed of 0.75 c

blocks.prompt: 81 The mass of an object moving at 0.96 c, in terms of its rest mass mₒ, is about:

book_ref.quote: Find the mass m of a moving object with speed 0.8 c.
